meta.title: Who really said "The Existence of Forgetting Has Never Been Proved"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not De Quincey — the thought is Nietzsche's Daybreak §126 (1881). The familiar English wording comes from a 1966 anthology, not the 1911 or 1997 translation.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The Existence of Forgetting Has Never Been Proved'?
meta.ogDescription: Nietzsche wrote it in 1881, not De Quincey — and the wording you know is a 1966 anthology's phrasing, matching neither the 1911 nor the 1997 translation.

answer.label: Not Thomas De Quincey — actually Friedrich Nietzsche
answer.sourceLine: The thought is Nietzsche’s, from aphorism 126 — headed “Forgetfulness” — of Morgenröthe (1881), the book published in English as The Dawn of Day or Daybreak. The familiar English wording, though, matches neither of the two English translations Quote Investigator sets against it — J. M. Kennedy’s 1911 version and a 1997 Cambridge rendering: it is the form printed in W. H. Auden and Louis Kronenberger’s The Viking Book of Aphorisms (1966) and credited there to Nietzsche. Thomas De Quincey wrote a different sentence on the same theme in 1821, which is almost certainly why his name gets attached.

source.heading: The Dawn of Day, aphorism 126

J. M. Kennedy, 1911 (quoted below) — the popular English wording matches neither Kennedy nor the 1997 Cambridge rendering

source.excerpt: Forgetfulness.—It has never yet been proved that there is such a thing as forgetfulness: all that we know is that we have no power over recollection. In the meantime we have filled up this gap in our power with the word “forgetfulness,” exactly as if it were another faculty added to our list. But, after all, what is within our power? If that word fills up a gap in our power, might not the other words be found capable of filling up a gap in the knowledge which we possess of our power?
trail: 1821 — Thomas De Quincey publishes Confessions of an English Opium-Eater in The London Magazine, containing a different sentence on the same theme: “there is no such thing as forgetting possible to the mind.” It is reprinted for decades and widely quoted — full text at Project Gutenberg ↗.

1881 — Nietzsche publishes Morgenröthe. Aphorism 126, headed “Forgetfulness,” makes the argument the modern quotation compresses; J. M. Kennedy’s 1911 translation renders it on page 131 — read it at Project Gutenberg ↗.

1960–1966 — the modern phrasing surfaces. Milon Brown’s Effective Work Management (1960) invokes Nietzsche without quotation marks; Auden and Kronenberger’s The Viking Book of Aphorisms (1966) prints the near-exact line, credited to Nietzsche — Quote Investigator’s citations ↗.

1967–1984 — the anthology wording spreads: an unattributed filler item in Texas’s Winters Enterprise (1967), a Nietzsche credit in The Kansas City Star (1972), and an epigraph to the memory chapter of a 1984 psychology textbook — all documented by QI ↗.
source.excerptNote: That is the complete aphorism as J. M. Kennedy rendered it in 1911, on page 131. The version that circulates today — “the existence of forgetting has never been proved” — compresses the first clause and drops the rest, and its phrasing comes from a 1966 anthology rather than from Kennedy or from the 1997 Cambridge rendering Quote Investigator sets beside him. (Those are the two translations QI compares; we have not checked every English translation of the book.)

source.rightsNote: Two different things are in play here. Nietzsche’s German original (1881) and J. M. Kennedy’s translation (1911) are both long in the public domain in the United States, and the excerpt above is quoted from Kennedy. The popular English wording is not: its earliest documented near-exact appearance is the entry in The Viking Book of Aphorisms (Viking Press, 1966), so we treat that specific rendering conservatively as in copyright rather than assume it descends from a pre-1931 translation.

author.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
author.heading: About Friedrich Nietzsche
author.bio: Nietzsche was a German philosopher and writer who began his career as a classical philologist, taking a chair at Basel while still in his twenties before ill health drove him out of academic life. Morgenröthe (1881) — The Dawn of Day, later Daybreak — is the book in which he said he opened his campaign against morality, and it is built from more than five hundred short numbered sections rather than continuous argument. That aphoristic form is exactly why lines like this one travel so easily: each section is already quotable, already detached from its surroundings.

copyAttribution: "The existence of forgetting has never been proved: we only know that some things do not come to mind when we want them." — Friedrich Nietzsche, not Thomas De Quincey. The thought is aphorism 126, "Forgetfulness," of Morgenröthe (1881), published in English as The Dawn of Day; J. M. Kennedy's 1911 translation reads "It has never yet been proved that there is such a thing as forgetfulness: all that we know is that we have no power over recollection." The familiar English wording above matches neither the 1911 Kennedy translation nor the 1997 Cambridge rendering Quote Investigator sets beside it — it is the form printed in W. H. Auden and Louis Kronenberger's The Viking Book of Aphorisms (Viking Press, 1966), p. 361, and credited there to Nietzsche. De Quincey's own line, from Confessions of an English Opium-Eater (1821), is different: "there is no such thing as forgetting possible to the mind."

misattribution.heading: Where the De Quincey credit comes from
misattribution.intro: Two writers phrased an idea about forgetting memorably, sixty years and one language apart, and the two sentences have been quietly merging ever since.

items.why: De Quincey did write about forgetting, and the line is famous — but it is a different sentence: “Of this at least I feel assured, that there is no such thing as forgetting possible to the mind,” from Confessions of an English Opium-Eater (1821), readable in full at Project Gutenberg ↗. Quote Investigator calls it a thematic precursor, not the source.

items.who: the 1911 or 1997 translations Quote Investigator compares
items.why: Neither translation QI prints reads this way. Kennedy’s 1911 version has “forgetfulness” and “no power over recollection”; a 1997 Cambridge University Press rendering has “the act of recollection does not lie within our power.” The familiar wording is the entry printed in the 1966 Viking Book of Aphorisms, per Quote Investigator’s citations ↗.

items.who: W. H. Auden and Louis Kronenberger
items.why: They compiled the 1966 anthology in which the modern wording first appears in near-exact form, and they credited it to Nietzsche — but a compiler’s name on the spine is not an author’s name on the line. QI lists both men among the candidate attributions ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea and the sentence are Nietzsche’s, from aphorism 126 of Morgenröthe (1881) — confirmed in the 1911 translation ↗. De Quincey’s line is his own, and it is not this one.

context.heading: Why the two lines keep collapsing into one
lead: Nietzsche’s point in aphorism 126 is not really about memory — it is about vocabulary. We have no reliable command over recollection, he argues, and rather than admit the gap in our powers we drop a noun into it, “forgetfulness,” and then treat the noun as though it named a faculty we possess. The closing question turns the knife: if one word papers over a hole in our power, how many other words are papering over holes in what we know about our power?

De Quincey had reached a neighbouring idea from the opposite direction in 1821, under opium, convinced that nothing is ever truly erased and that a veil merely falls between us and “the secret inscriptions on the mind.” Both lines say something like forgetting is not what you think it is, both are short, and both are endlessly reprinted — which is a reliable recipe for one man’s sentence ending up under the other man’s name. The modern psychology of memory made the collision worse: the anthology wording was used as the epigraph to the memory chapter of a 1984 psychology textbook, and it now circulates in exactly the contexts where the retrieval-failure reading is being argued.
detailsBody: 1911, J. M. Kennedy’s translation: “It has never yet been proved that there is such a thing as forgetfulness: all that we know is that we have no power over recollection.”
1997, a Cambridge University Press rendering: “It has not yet been proved that there is any such thing as forgetting; all we know is that the act of recollection does not lie within our power.”

1966, The Viking Book of Aphorisms: “The existence of forgetting has never been proved: we only know that some things do not come to our mind when we want them to.” — the version everyone now quotes, minus the “our” and the trailing “to.”
context.pull: we have filled up this gap in our power with the word “forgetfulness”

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the saying derives from Nietzsche's 1881 Morgenröthe §126; prints the 1911 Kennedy and 1997 Cambridge translations; identifies the 1966 Viking Book of Aphorisms (p. 361) as the near-exact match to the modern wording credited to Nietzsche; lists the 1960 Milon Brown paraphrase, 1967 Winters Enterprise filler, 1972 Kansas City Star, and 1984 psychology textbook epigraph; and calls De Quincey's 1821 line a thematic precursor rather than the source.

J. M. Kennedy's 1911 translation of The Dawn of Day contains aphorism 126, headed 'Forgetfulness': 'It has never yet been proved that there is such a thing as forgetfulness: all that we know is that we have no power over recollection...' The title page reads 'Translated by John McFarland Kennedy... New York, The MacMillan Company, 1911.'
The scanned printed edition of Kennedy's The Dawn of Day shows section 126 ('FORGETFULNESS. It has never yet been proved that there is such a thing as forgetfulness...') on page 131.

De Quincey's Confessions of an English Opium-Eater contains: 'Of this at least I feel assured, that there is no such thing as forgetting possible to the mind; a thousand accidents may and will interpose a veil between our present consciousness and the secret inscriptions on the mind...'

The Dawn of Day is an 1881 book by Friedrich Nietzsche, originally titled 'Morgenröthe – Gedanken über die moralischen Vorurtheile', with English translations including J. M. Kennedy's and R. J. Hollingdale's Daybreak.
Friedrich Wilhelm Nietzsche (15 October 1844 – 25 August 1900) was a German philosopher and writer who started his career as a classical philologist.
